Negative reinforcement removing an unpleasant task

qs.q: While preparing for an emergency exploratory laparotomy, a surgeon notes that their hands are not visibly soiled. Which of the following describes the correct duration and method for hand hygiene using an alcohol-based rub?
o: Massaged vigorously from fingertips to the elbows for 2 minutes
Applied for 40 to 60 seconds concentrating only on the palms
Scrubbed with antiseptic soap and a brush for up to 5 minutes
Applied for 20 to 30 seconds following all anatomical steps
qs.e: An alcohol-based rub applied for 20 to 30 seconds following all steps is effective when hands are not visibly soiled. Antiseptic soap scrubbing for 2 to 5 minutes is reserved for surgical scrubbing.

es.q: Discuss the principles of hand hygiene, including social hand wash and surgical scrubbing.
es.m:
- **Prevention:** Hand washing is the single most important measure for the prevention of infection.
- **Social hand wash:** Plain soap and water removes visible contamination by washing with vigorous mechanical action on all hand surfaces for at least 40 to 60 seconds, including above the wrists; jewellery and watches must be removed.
- **Greatest contamination:** Nails are the areas of greatest contamination and must be cleaned thoroughly.
- **Hand rub:** An alcohol-based rub applied for 20 to 30 seconds following all steps (palms, backs, between the fingers, fingertips, thumbs, wrists) is effective when hands are not visibly soiled.

es.q: List and explain the hand hygiene steps required as part of aseptic technique.
es.m:
**Hand hygiene requirements:**
- Wash hands thoroughly before handling any cultures or samples.
- Wash hands thoroughly after handling cultures or samples.
- Use proper washing technique to remove potential contaminants from the skin.
- Perform hand hygiene each time the hands may become contaminated during laboratory work.

ai.title: Hand Hygiene in Low-Resource Settings
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Hand hygiene reduces transmission of pathogens in hospitals. In low-resource settings, soap and water or alcohol rubs are key. Clinicians must assess barriers, educate staff, and monitor compliance to protect patients.

sections.p: Hand hygiene is the cornerstone of infection prevention. It interrupts the hand–surface–patient cycle that spreads bacteria, viruses and fungi, especially in busy wards with limited resources.
b: Key principles: before patient contact, after contact, after removing gloves, after contact with bodily fluids, after touching contaminated surfaces.

sections.p: Most hospital-acquired infections are caused by gram‑positive cocci (Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase‑negative staphylococci), gram‑negative rods (Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas), and fungi (Candida).
b: These organisms survive on skin and surfaces for hours to days; hand hygiene removes them before they reach vulnerable patients.

sections.p: Pathogens are transferred by direct contact or via contaminated surfaces. Hands act as vectors, picking up organisms from patients, equipment or the environment.
b: In low‑resource settings, frequent hand contamination occurs due to high patient load, limited glove supply, and inadequate cleaning supplies.

sections.p: Inadequate hand hygiene leads to outbreaks of neonatal sepsis, surgical site infections, catheter‑associated urinary tract infections, and multidrug‑resistant organism transmission.
b: Neonatal sepsis is a leading cause of infant mortality in East Africa; most cases are preventable with proper hand hygiene.

sections.p: Clinical diagnosis relies on identifying infection signs (fever, wound erythema, urinary symptoms). Laboratory confirmation is limited but may include culture of wound swabs or urine.
b: In settings without culture, clinical judgment and empirical treatment guided by local antibiograms are essential.

sections.p: Control focuses on prevention: enforce hand hygiene, use alcohol rubs where water is scarce, provide training, and monitor compliance.
b: When alcohol rubs are unavailable, handwashing with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds is effective.

sections.p: Examiners often ask about the WHO 5 moments of hand hygiene, barriers in low‑resource settings, and how to audit compliance.
b: Remember the 5 moments: before touching patient, before clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure, after touching patient, after touching patient surroundings.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe sepsis, sudden deterioration after a procedure, or signs of a hospital outbreak (cluster of infections).

faq.q: What is the best hand hygiene method when water is scarce?
faq.a: Use alcohol‑based hand rub (≥60% alcohol) for at least 20 seconds; if unavailable, wash with soap and water for 20 seconds.

faq.q: How can I audit hand hygiene compliance?
faq.a: Use direct observation, check soap/alcohol availability, and review infection rates; provide feedback and education to staff.
